title: Stephan James on Honoring Carl Weathers’ Legacy and Learning to Box for ‘I Play Rocky’
description: Stephan James has played a few real-life figures in his career, including Olympic gold medalist Jesse Owens (in 2016’s “Race”) and civil rights lead
body:
Stephan James has played a few real-life figures in his career, including Olympic gold medalist Jesse Owens (in 2016’s “Race”) and civil rights leader John Lewis (2014’s “Selma”), so he knows the drill. Diving deep into the archives for research. Vocal coaching. Perhaps a physical transformation.

	His mission: honor the man, the mythic character he originated and their combined legacy. (Weathers died in 2024 at 76.)


	“It’s not lost on me, just how important Carl Weathers was not only in this franchise, but what he represented as a young Black leading man during that era,” James tells Variety, sitting down for an extensive interview about the role. “So, I just wanted to do that person justice and give him as many colors as I could in the short amount of time that I had in this film.”
	

	Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” now playing in theaters nationwide, focuses on the unbelievable true story of how Sylvester Stallone (portrayed by Anthony Ippolito) came to write “Rocky” and ultimately play the title role. But as much as the movie focuses on Stallone’s star-making moment, it also spotlights the key casting of Weathers, a former pro football star, who’d played bit parts on shows like “Good Times,” “The Six Million Dollar Man” and “Kung Fu.”

	James shines in the character’s introduction scene: a crackling sequence in which Weathers auditions to play Apollo Creed, the heavyweight champ whom Stallone’s underdog Rocky will fight. James’ Weathers struts in with his shirt unbuttoned to reveal impressively toned abs. When the casting director asks his age, he quips: “Honey, I’m young as the sun and old as spit. Whatever, you need me to be.” It’s all going swimmingly — he delivers his lines with panache; he’s got experience in the boxing ring (a fib, but we’ll get to that later) — until it’s time to read with a mumbling Stallone. 
	

	“Look, can we cut?” Weathers says, leaping to his feet to complain about his scene partner. “I would really do better if I had a real actor reading with me, goddamnit.” When he’s informed that Stallone is the writer and lead actor of the picture, he replies, slyly: “Well maybe he’ll get better.”



	The fine-tuned comedy is a different look for the 32-year-old Canadian star, best known for dramatic parts — like “If Beale Street Could Talk,” “Homecoming,” “The Piano Lesson” and “Ricky” — and he plays it all with a mischievous glint in his eye. 

	“He’s got so much presence. He’s so magnetic that it wasn’t hard,” James says about filming the sequence. “I just tried to step into the best version of myself, tap into all the presence and charm that I have — and it’s not as much as him — but, trying to take what was within me and just compounding on top of it.”



	

					Stephan James and Anthony Ippolito at the world premiere of “I Play Rocky” during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival; Sylvester Stallone and Carl Weathers in “Rocky.”
									2026 Getty Images / ©United Artists/Courtesy Everett Collection
	



	While “I Play Rocky” coincides with the 50th anniversary of the original “Rocky,” the movie also comes after Creed’s legacy has been pushed to the forefront of the franchise thanks to Michael B. Jordan and Ryan Coogler’s blockbuster “Creed” trilogy. During the press run, James joked about calling up his “son” Jordan (as the Oscar winner’s Adonis Creed is the love child of the late boxing champ) to talk about the family business. 

	“I’ll tell you the truth: I did not call Mike, and we did not have this discussion,” James says, laughing. “But, I will say that I’m happy to be in the family.”

	To prepare for the role, James dropped between 20 and 25 pounds in two months and learned how to box for real. Read on for more about how he prepared for the part and the question he wishes he could’ve asked Weathers before production.
	
		One of the gags in the film is that Carl Weather claimed to know how to box, but he really didn’t. Is there anything on in the special skills section of resume that you’ve embellished?	

	The list is far too long for the 10 minutes that we have right now.
	
		Well, good news, we have 20.	

	Oh OK, cool. If I’m being honest, yeah, there are little white lies that you tell to help set yourself up for success. You don’t want to get caught in those lies too, though. So you want to make sure you can sort of deliver on it. Or that by the time they catch you in the lie, they love you so much that it doesn’t matter.
	
	
		When I talk to actors, the one that always seems to come up is they say they can ride a horse, and when they get on set, the producers find out they’ve never been near a horse.	

	Yep, I’ll say I ride a horse. I own a horse. I’ve even put that on my resume. So, you know, whatever you got to do.
	
		Wait, you actually own a horse? Or you just put it on your resume?	

	See, you believe me. That was good, right?
	
		I mean, why would you lie to me? To that point, what was the key to nailing Carl’s swagger in that audition scene?	

	More than anything, it was just fun. So many times when you’re performing, I’ll have moments where I’m like, ‘Oh, I can’t even be around anyone,’ or I’m so locked in and so hyper focused on lines, or trying to stay in a in a vibe or a mood. That wasn’t this [movie] for me. This was Peter Farrelly giving me the keys to the scene and being like, ‘Go do your thing.’ So, it was very rewarding to see how it finally turned out.
	
		Peter has said that he did not want to do this movie without you. That once he knew that you were a possibility to play the role, it needed to be you for this. How did this part come to you?	

	I just got a call from my manager, like most things, that they’re making this movie and that they were looking for Carl Weathers. And I was like, ‘Carl Weathers, yes. Where do I sign up?’ It didn’t take any convincing. I read the script. I was blown away by it. I put my tape together for Pete, and he liked it.
	
		What made you so quick to say yes? You’ve played Jesse Owens, John Lewis, so many of our real-life heroes, but it is always intimidating to step into someone’s shoes. So why were you like, “No, I cannot let this role pass me by.”	

	There’s an internal litmus test that a lot of actors have. Maybe they’ll admit it. Maybe they won’t. But a part of it is when you read something and you’re like, “I don’t want to see anyone else do this.” Like, “I feel like I have the most to add to it or bring to it, and I don’t want to see anybody else’s version of this. I want to do my version.” So, that was a big deciding factor. Just reading it and being like, “No, it’s too special” on the page; I want to be able to do it myself. These characters that mean so much, that are so impactful, it’s an honor. It’s like why wouldn’t I want to have that you know on my belt if you will, that I got to play Carl Weathers. It’s amazing!
	
	
		That’s a boxing championship belt in and of itself. What was one of the key stories that you read, listened to or got from someone that really helped you tap into Carl’s character?	

	His warmth was something that people don’t really get to see too much. Just looking at him, he could come across as like this physically imposing, maybe scary individual, but I’ve spoken to people who’ve spent a lot of real time with him, and you know they’ve all said just how kind he was.

	I tried to add that into the film just in terms of his relationship with Sly. When he finally admits that he’s not a boxer, and the fact that they could both laugh at that moment and then bond on something like, “Yes, we’re adversaries in this film, but, for the purposes of making this film, we’re gonna have to lock in and be able to trust each other, and it’d be nice if we liked each other too.”



	

					Anthony Ippolito (as Sylvester Stallone) and Stephen James (as Carl Weathers) in “I Play Rocky.”
									©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collection
	


	
		You never got to meet Carl. What is one question you wish you could ask him?	

	I’d be keen to know if he really understood what he would mean to the legacy of this franchise, not only in the four “Rocky” films he made, but, if you count the “Creed” films [too]. The fact that there was a whole other world that spawned off people’s love for you and your character and your lineage, that we can make a whole series of movies about his son now.

	That really is Carl Weathers and his legacy. Not every actor rather is going to step into that role and last for four movies and then [influence] three more after that. Like, that’s because of him. So, I would wonder if he knew on those first days on “Rocky I,” like, did you ever think it could be this?
	
		That’s an incredible question because I can’t imagine that they did. This was all just a labor of love — a great story, a great script, great opportunity. And it’s turned into this massive, multi-generational franchise. You did do your own boxing training for this. What did your process look like?	

	I was just over 200 pounds when I found out that I got this job and I found out that I had two months to get ready for this. So, my initial thought process was, “Let me just start eating and bulking up,” like protein for breakfast, lunch and dinner, just go ham. And I spoke to a trainer friend of mine, and he said, if you work on cutting your body fat percentage down, effectively losing weight while keeping your muscle, you’ll be great. And people are gonna think you look bigger than you actually are. Trust me.
	

	So, that became my process: weight training at the gym in the morning; going down to Kingsway Boxing Club in Toronto with my trainer Jennifer Huggins and we just took it day by day, step by step. It started with cardio, just getting my endurance level up, then it was footwork. I didn’t realize how big footwork was in boxing. Just learning how to not move around like a baby deer. And then unlearning all of those things to be the unpolished version of Apollo Creed. There were layers and levels to it. By the time I was done, I ended up dropping like 20-25 pounds and in the film, I’m 170-175 max.
	
		How much fun did you have going toe to toe with Anthony recreating these epic boxing scenes?	

	I’m still healing from some of the punches I took, but it was a lot of fun to work with Anthony and spend so much time with him. Just getting close with him, building like a bond and a level of trust with each other. That’s crucial, time for character development. For us to actually be going through the motions of the choreography in that last fight scene, getting into the psychology of what it meant to be a boxer and respecting that art form, the process was equally as important as the filming itself.
	
		After this, you’re heading off to star in “Discretion,” a legal drama with Nicole Kidman and Elle Fanning. What have what have you enjoyed about going into that realm?	

	First of all, I wear like the greatest suits ever, so that’s really fly. They’re all like custom made, so hopefully the production will give them to me afterward, because like who else are they gonna fit? So that’s been really really cool.

	And then, just playing this young, smart, quick-witted lawyer has been really fun. I just feel like I’m stepping outside of myself and again giving the world something that they haven’t really seen me in.



	

					Anthony Ippolito (as Sylvester Stallone) and Stephen James (as Carl Weathers) in “I Play Rocky,” opposite Weathers and Stallone from “Rocky.”
									Courtesy Everett Collection / ©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collection

	Actor Awards Predictions: Andrew Garfield, Inde Navarrette and ‘The Odyssey’ Lead an Unsettled Film Race as ‘Widow’s Bay’ and HBO Max Could Rule TV
	



			
			
	
						

									Neon
	
					


							
		

	Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predictions for the upcoming Oscars, Emmys, Grammys and Tony Awards ceremonies, curated by Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis. The prediction pages reflect the current standings in the race and do not reflect personal preferences for any individual contender. As other formal (and informal) polls suggest, competitions are fluid and subject to change based on buzz and events. Predictions are updated every Thursday.



	

					OBSESSION, Inde Navarrette
									©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection
	




	2027 Actor Awards Predictions Commentary All Categories (Updated: Nov. 21, 2026): Seven. That’s how many nominations “The Odyssey” is projected to collect, which would tie the all-time record for a film at the Actor Awards, going back to the SAG Awards days. That record is only a year old, when “One Battle After Another” earned a record-breaking seven nods last season. Christopher Nolan’s epic is projected to land: cast ensemble, stunt ensemble, Matt Damon in lead and four supporting slots split between John Leguizamo, Robert Pattinson, Anne Hathaway and Samantha Morton.

	Andrew Garfield’s turn as Sam Altman is the early favorite for “Artificial” that could bring him his first trophy. Breakout Inde Navarrette would be the season’s most unlikely lead actress nominee and maybe its most deserved with her possessed girlfriend in “Obsession” carrying a microbudget horror film to the top of Focus Features’ box office history. If there’s any place that can truly challenge Julianne Moore’s remarkable turn in “The Debut,” it’s here.

	And noteworthy reminder, Amanda Seyfried is not eligible here for “You Can See Everything.”

	On the TV side, HBO Max takes 13 of the 45 projected slots and “The Pitt” returns as the reigning drama ensemble champ. Last season, Noah Wyle made history by winning all five major acting awards in one season for his role as Dr. Robby, and he could do it again. But the most-nominated series isn’t predicted to be the medical drama. It’s “Widow’s Bay,” Apple TV’s comedy, with five: ensemble, stunts, O’Flynn and a potential head-to-head in lead comedy between Matthew Rhys and Stephen Root. That matches the total from last year, when “The Studio” led TV with 5 noms. “DTF St. Louis” and “The Diplomat” follow with three each, and the drama actress race may be the one to watch. Keri Russell, who earned the honor for Best Actress in a Drama Series for “The Diplomat” last year, is back in the lineup, but she’ll have to fight off newcomer Emmy Rossum (“Furious”) to take her title.

	Actor nominations will be announced Wednesday, Jan. 13, 2027.

title: Andrew Rannells Was Told to ‘Stay Away’ From Kevin Spacey After Meeting Backstage at ‘The Book of Mormon’; He Then Sent a ‘Handwritten Letter’ ‘Asking Me on a Date’
description:
Andrew Rannells recently revealed that Kevin Spacey asked him out while the “Girls” actor was starring in “The Book of Mormon” on Broadway.

	“I’ve
body:
Andrew Rannells recently revealed that Kevin Spacey asked him out while the “Girls” actor was starring in “The Book of Mormon” on Broadway.

	“I’ve never told this story before. He asked me on a date once,” Rannells said while guesting on “The Downside” podcast hosted by Gianmarco Soresi. “He sent me a letter to ‘The Book of Mormon.’ Handwritten.” The actors went on to explain that the Oscar winner came to see the musical and “came backstage” to meet him after the show.
	

	“There were always a lot of really fun people there, but sometimes they would bring them up into our dressing rooms, but with no notice,” he said. “So after the show, we’re getting changed. There’s a knock on my door. It was Goldie Hawn, Kevin Spacey, and Joel Schumacher. They were not together, but they all walked up together. So then we were all crammed in my dressing room.”

	Rannells continued: “Kevin Spacey was sort of rubbing my neck as we were standing there… Joel Schumacher, who was very close to me, he said, ‘Stay away from that man.’” That prompted Spacey to respond, “Hey! C’mon, c’mon,” he recalled. “And then like a week later, I got a handwritten letter from him asking me on a date.” Rannells concluded by noting he “never responded” to the note.

	Rannells originated the role of Elder Price in the long-running musical, performing from the show’s opening in 2011 through June 2012. The part earned him a Tony nomination for best leading actor in a musical. 

	Spacey’s sexual assault allegations came years later in 2017, when fellow Broadway actor Anthony Rapp said that the actor assaulted him in his New York apartment while Rapp was a teenager. Rapp later filed a $40 million civil lawsuit for sexual assault and battery in 2022, but a New York jury found Spacey not liable on all counts. Earlier this year, Spacey reached a settlement with three men who sued him over sexual assault claims, avoiding a civil trial in London that was set for October.

title: Celluloid Sounds: Fewer Women Composers on Screen, But Some Hit the Right Notes
description: The stats for women composers in Hollywood have not improved. Just eight of this year’s top 100 grossing films feature original scores by women; th
body:
The stats for women composers in Hollywood have not improved. Just eight of this year’s top 100 grossing films feature original scores by women; the past two years have seen percentages between 7 and 9%, all down from 14% in 2023.

	But female composers continue to be in the awards conversation, and not all for their music. Laura Karpman, composer of “American Fiction” and the current Netflix miniseries “East of Eden,” has entered her first film as director in the documentary short subject category: “Cosmic Symphony.”
	

	The film is a timely look at four musical artists who lost priceless, beloved instruments in the Palisades and Eaton fires of January 2025: composer Starr Parodi, whose 1928 Steinway piano was heard in dozens of MGM scores including “The Wizard of Oz”; songwriter Diane Warren, who lost a Yamaha grand; jazz bassist John Clayton, whose string bass was nearly 200 years old; and Altadena educator Susie Chung, whose brown Steinway was played by Lady Gaga in “A Star Is Born” and on the 2019 Oscarcast.

	“I believe my piano has a soul… I have a little regret that I left her alone,” Chung says in the film, and that sentiment is echoed by the other musicians. “Instruments have hearts, they have souls, they have lives,” says Warren, a 17-time best song nominee. Two days before the fires, Warren was filmed performing her Oscar-nominated song “The Journey” on the piano in her Malibu beach house.

	Clayton’s bass, once owned by the legendary Ray Brown, had accompanied Ella Fitzgerald, Frank Sinatra, Nat King Cole and Duke Ellington. Recalling its past, he said “that bass and the music that it made was bigger than any of us could ever be.”
	

	Parodi describes her lost keyboard as having “this beautiful, haunting, bell-like sound… warm and thick,” and she tells the harrowing story of watching her house go up in flames via their doorbell camera and later unearthing the remains of her MGM piano in the rubble.

	Thousands of instruments were reduced to ash during the L.A. fires. “I felt it was a story that was really important to be told,” Karpman says. “When you live with these instruments, they have personalities, they see history.”

	In addition to the interviews and performance footage, she added lively, colorful animation to the story. Animator Tempe Hale sought “to make the instruments come alive again, (to convey) the kind of fun and glory and energy that these instruments have.”

	Karpman also composed the score for her film, incorporating both orchestral and choral sounds to suggest the music still being made, in the beyond, by those lost music makers.

	Scottish composer Anna Meredith wrote one of the year’s most unusual scores for the romantic fantasy “Wicker,” which stars Olivia Colman as a fisherwoman and Alexander Skarsgård as her artificial husband, made for her by a basket weaver in their medieval village.

	The entire score is played by just four people: a violist, a cellist, a recorder player and Meredith herself. “I’d much rather start small with a tiny lens, and see what you can do with it, rather than have every sound in the world, where it could just sound like any old thing. You have to really think creatively,” she says.

	Directors Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson reached out to Meredith during shooting (to write music for a wedding scene), and she quickly became part of a team that included several women in key roles (including editor Sofi Marshall). The composer decided that the timeframe and the nature of the story demanded wooden instruments for a “timeless quality.”

	Meredith used as many as 10 different recorders, “from tiny little baby ones, only 20 centimeters; lots of ones in the conventional treble tenor range; and some bonkers instruments, including a bass one and a contrabass one which was so tall we had to move to a different recording studio. We had to find one with a skylight to fit the neck of that one, like seven feet tall.”
	

	The recorders represented the fisherwoman and her wicker husband, while the strings (the darker sounds of viola and cello) represented the villagers. “It’s not nice string sounds,” she says, “it’s slithery, nasty sounds. Their sound worlds are, initially, kept quite different, and then the strings sort of ‘infect’ the recorders as the villagers start to impose on their relationship.”

	The directors “wanted the score to be bold,” Meredith adds, “and it’s loud as well. The music is upfront. I’m very proud to be part of a film with a strong female story and so many important female elements, both on and off the screen, that have been part of it.”

	For “Tenzing,” the untold story of the Nepalese-Indian Sherpa who accompanied Edmund Hillary to the top of Mount Everest in 1953, Norwegian-born, Stockholm-based composer Rebekka Karijord insisted on cultural authenticity. “I felt, early on, that we needed to have a collaboration with Nepalese musicians that isn’t like an exotic tone or a color,” she says. “It had to be a deep collaboration.”

	She enlisted a Nepalese spiritual leader and Buddhist nun, Ani Choying Drolma, to contribute traditional Buddhist chants; Nepal’s premier flautist and throat singer Manose Singh; and actress Thinley Lhamo, who plays Tenzing’s wife Dawa in the film and is also a highly regarded singer of Tibetan opera.

	Lhamo “has the most amazing voice,” Karijord says. That voice becomes, in a sense, the sound of the mountain itself. “I wanted to have something that could transcend the physical effort, that could pull us into the spiritual aspect, and her voice really solved that for me throughout the score.”

	In addition, she had the sound team record a number of unique sounds from the region—yak bells, goat bells, the sound of prayer wheels in the temples, Tibetan singing bowls and gongs—which she and her percussionist sampled and added to her musical library for incorporation into the score.

	The film details England’s drive to be the first nation to reach the summit of the world’s tallest peak, Karijord points out. “It needed the big cinematic muscles, a meeting between Western and Eastern. If I could make the mountain, this goddess, beautiful and pristine and dangerous and magnetizing, then we will understand why’re drawn to her—both Tenzing as a little boy growing up at the foot of the mountain, and these Englishmen wanting to conquer it.”
	

	Karijord employed a 40-piece string section from the London Contemporary Orchestra, in part to convey the danger of crevasses, avalanches and rumbles in the ice, along with a handful of woodwind and brass players and a 12-voice choir. Textural elements, such as the sound of breathing, also became a factor in the score.

	Regarding the few female composers scoring studio films, Karijord notes that “it’s such a deeply empathetic craft to score films, and it’s a deeply collaborative craft. I know a lot of women who are both very empathetic and collaborative and brave. So I think there should be more of us doing it.”

schema.headline: Celluloid Sounds: Fewer Women Composers on Screen, But Some Hit the Right Notes

title: CAA’s Bryan Lourd Urges Congress to Pass NO FAKES Act to Combat AI Deepfakes: ‘Every One of Us Should Have the Right to Say No’
description: Creative Arts Agency CEO Bryan Lourd urged Congress on Saturday to pass the NO FAKES Act, a bill that would regulate the wave of unauthorized AI de
body:
Creative Arts Agency CEO Bryan Lourd urged Congress on Saturday to pass the NO FAKES Act, a bill that would regulate the wave of unauthorized AI deepfakes proliferating the internet, writing in a New York Times Opinion piece that “every one of us should have the right to say no to an unwelcome use of our likeness.”

	The NO FAKES Act was introduced by Sen. Chris Coons (D-ME) in May, following a previous attempt at the bill last year. While it advanced out of the Senate Judiciary Committee in June and has a bipartisan coalition of co-sponsors, the full Senate has not taken it up. Lourd wrote that the bill would introduce a federal standard for “control, consent and compensation” surrounding deepfakes, replacing “outdated, ill-fitting state laws, many of them written with an analog world in mind.”
	

	“I come to this issue not as a policymaker but as a practitioner. I run a global talent agency. Part of our job is to help our clients license their likenesses and performances, sometimes to AI companies,” he added. “We regularly negotiate those deals, and I can tell you that the bill pending in Congress delivers what the industry needs and what will protect all Americans.”

	Lourd laid out the stakes for Hollywood by citing Tom Hanks, who warned his followers in 2023 about a dental office using an AI deepfake of a younger version of him in an advertisement. Hanks likely wouldn’t have agreed to the dental ad, Lourd wrote, but he should’ve been given a choice before the dental office ran with an unauthorized deepfake.

	“What’s missing is a bright-line rule affirming that right in the AI age, and it is one Congress can supply before the year is out,” Lourd wrote.
	

	CAA has advocated against the unauthorized proliferation of celebrity deepfakes online, working with the Cate Blanchett-backed Human Consent Foundation to help people control permissions for their likenesses if they’re scraped by AI models. The agency also joined the foundation and other entertainment backers in an amicus brief in the New York Times’ lawsuit against OpenAI, noting the active licensing market for likenesses that’s developed in the AI era.

	Deepfakes have been a constant presence since large-language models emerged in 2022, with many being used to produce unauthorized and sometimes explicit depictions of actors, singers and other celebrities. Other industry backers of the NO FAKES Act include SAG-AFTRA, the Motion Picture Association, the Recording Industry Association of America, the Recording Academy and the National Association of Broadcasters, OpenAI, the AFL-CIO, YouTube and IBM.

title: Liz Daly Byrne, Model and Wife of PMC Vice Chairman Gerry Byrne, Dies at 81
description:
Liz Daly Byrne, a model and philanthropist who was married to PMC vice chairman Gerry Byrne for more than 55 years, has died. She was 81.

	Byrne f
body:
Liz Daly Byrne, a model and philanthropist who was married to PMC vice chairman Gerry Byrne for more than 55 years, has died. She was 81.

	Byrne faced a battle with cancer three years ago, and recently learned that her illness had returned. She had faced recurring complications from severe injuries suffered in a bicycle accident in 2000. Byrne died Nov. 17 after a period of home hospice care in New York.


	Byrne was active as a philanthropist and social advocate through her work with the United Nations’ Operation Smile campaign, traveling internationally with the organization on medical missions. She had long been involved in causes to support military families and veterans. Byrne was remembered by her family, including her adult children, digital entrepreneur Gavin Byrne and actor Megan Byrne, as a woman who embodied “elegance, strength, wit, faith, generosity and compassion.” 
	

	Byrne was also extremely fast on her feet, as she demonstrated in 1997 during the Cannes Film Festival. During a post-screening party for Warner Bros./New Regency’s buzzy period drama “L.A. Confidential” at a vineyard, a tipsy guest fell into the pool. As Variety reported, when Byrne saw what had happened, she “threw off her jacket and shoes and dove into the water for a dramatic rescue, after which she calmly took her seat for the sit-down dinner at fireworks show.”

	Born in 1945, Byrne grew up in the shadow of Yankee Stadium in the Bronx. She met her future husband Gerry Byrne — who served as publisher of Variety from 1989 to 2000 and at present is vice chair of Variety parent company PMC — while he was attending Fordham College in the borough. The two were neighbors, but in a wonderfully Bronx love story touch, Liz Daly met Gerry Byrne one evening during a ride on the D train.
	

	Early on, Liz Daly was drawn to New York’s fashion world. She signed with top modeling agencies Mannequin and Ellen Harth and launched her career as the primary designer’s model for top New York retailers Saks Fifth Avenue and Bonwit Teller. In addition to appearing in TV commercials, Byrne spent years as a runway model with Anne Klein, Donna Karan, Oscar de la Renta and Bill Tice. She then spent another decade working with renowned designers Bob Mackie and Ray Aghayan.

	Daly and Byrne married in 1969 at the chapel at St. Patrick’s Cathedral, after Gerry Byrne completed a three-year tour with the U.S. Marine Corps in Vietnam. In tribute to her husband’s service, Liz Byrne successfully launched a POW bracelet program to honor the sacrifices made by some families. The effort took root after being publicized nationally through coverage in the New York Times.

	Byrne was a dedicated marathon runner who participated in multiple New York City Marathons as well as runs hosted by the Marines in Washington, D.C. She was active in numerous nonprofits and in entertainment and media industry charitable efforts.

	(Pictured: Liz Daly Byrne and Gerry Byrne in 2017)



	

					From the May 19, 1997, edition of Daily Variety

title: Box Office: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Scores $56 Million on Friday, ‘I Play Rocky’ Follows With $3.8 Million
description: The odds were ever in the favor of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” the latest entry in the storied franchise, which ruled the box offic
body:
The odds were ever in the favor of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” the latest entry in the storied franchise, which ruled the box office on Friday.

	“Sunrise on the Reaping” generated $56 million from 4,018 North American theaters on Friday, taking the No. 1 spot on its opening day. It’s a strong start for the prequel, which looks to pull in around $120 million by Sunday. (That number far exceeds the cautious $85 million start the studio had projected.)
	

	The Francis Lawrence-directed film takes place 25 years before the original “Hunger Games” series and follows the origin story of Haymitch Abernathy as he’s forced to compete in the second Quarter Quell. Joseph Zada, McKenna Grace, Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Elle Fanning and more star, with appearances from original “The Hunger Games” cast members Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson and Woodey Harleson.

	“Sunrise on the Reaping” is the second prequel in the series, following 2023’s “The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes,” which finished its theatrical run at $363 million globally, making it a commercial success against a $100 million budget. With the new release, the “Hunger Games” franchise has generated more than $3.437 billion at the worldwide box office.

	Amazon MGM’s “I Play Rocky” landed in second place on Friday, grossing $3.8 million from 2477 North American theaters following its wide expansion. The film is expected to gross $9.3 million by Sunday, bringing its cumulative total to $10.419 million. “I Play Rocky” previously brought in just under $1 million after two weekends in limited release.
	

	The biopic-type film tells the true story behind the tumultuous making of the 1976 boxing classic “Rocky.” Anthony Ippolito portrays a young Sylvester Stallone, with AnnaSophia Robb, Kiki Seto, Matt Dillon, Stephan James and more also starring.

	Paramount Pictures’ “Ebenezer” took the No. 3 spot with $2.04 million from 3,545 North American theaters in its second weekend in theaters. The Johnny Depp-led drama is eyeing another $7.775 million by Sunday, bringing its cumulative gross to $32.62 million.

	“Ebenezer” reimagines the Christmas classic “A Christmas Carol,” this time starring Depp as Scrooge. Directed by Ti West, the description simply reads: “The name you know, the story you don’t.” Alongside Depp, “Ebenezer” boasts an ensemble including Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley, Arthur Conti, Ellie Bamber, Henry Lloyd-Hughes, Charlie Murphy, Tramell Tillman and Ian McKellen.

	“The Cat in the Hat” followed in fourth place with $1.6 million from 3,26 locations. Rival estimates expect Warner Bros.’ animated film to add $7 million by Sunday, bringing the animated film’s cumulative gross to $47.26 million.

	Bill Hader voices the titular character in the cartoon, which follows the shenanigans that occur after a mischievous, hat-wearing cat arrives to cheer up two siblings who move to a new town.

	Finally, in fifth place was Columbia Pictures’ “Ghost Soldier.” The William Eubank-directed film earned $700,000 on Friday, coming in just ahead of GKids’ “Godzilla Minus Zero,” which brought in $680,000 on Friday. That puts the “Godzilla Minus One” follow-up at more than $51 million domestically.

title: An Iranian Woman Falls Pregnant to Avoid Execution in ‘Inherited’: Situation in Iran Is ‘Increasingly Complex’
description: A few years ago, Iranian filmmaker Morteza Alizadeh saw a photograph that he couldn’t shake from his mind: it showed mothers and their children goi
body:
A few years ago, Iranian filmmaker Morteza Alizadeh saw a photograph that he couldn’t shake from his mind: it showed mothers and their children going about their lives, which at first seemed routine, until the director realized it was taken inside a women’s prison.

	From that first glimpse into a little spoken-about reality, Alizadeh spent years researching how common it is for Iranian women to have children while waiting to be executed in prison. In “Inherited,” world premiering at the Cairo Film Festival, the director tells the fictional story of one of them, Mina (played by Mina Sadati). Sentenced to death for murder and running against the clock of her scheduled execution, she learns the only way to postpone her fate is to become pregnant.
	

	“My main goal with this film was to portray people who find themselves in difficult and sensitive situations, where they are forced to make choices to survive,” Alizadeh tells Variety. “These choices affect not only their own lives but, more importantly, the lives of others.”

	The director dedicated a long period to research, collecting an extensive archive of images from inside prisons, which included rare documentaries and footage from hacked surveillance cameras. He also spent months meeting and interviewing women who had been imprisoned and had either been released temporarily or were on leave. “With their help, we were able to design the entire prison environment in detail,” he notes. “Then our production design team recreated and built the whole prison set as closely as possible to the real thing.”
	

	By posing a complex moral conundrum when Mina’s family pleads with the unmarried prisoner to abort the baby to preserve the family’s honor, the director wanted the audience to “ask themselves” how much right “does one person have to decide another person’s fate.” “What gives us the authority to decide whether to take someone’s life or give another person the chance to live?”

	At the same time, it was important to me that the audience wouldn’t simply judge the characters for their choices, but would also try to understand the circumstances and the structures that put them in such difficult situations,” he adds.



	

	



	The film’s strong moral core and an unwillingness to offer easy answers speak to a long tradition of Iranian cinema established by names such as Jafar Panahi, Asghar Farhadi and Abbas Kiarostami. “I believe the roots of this cinematic tradition, of creating morally complex situations, can be found in Iranian society and its social and cultural conditions,” says Alizadeh.

	In that sense, the director feels a “deep connection” between “Inherited” and the work of his countrymen, which all come from a “shared reality of Iranian society” and are “influenced by the circumstances we live in.” “The experiences, contradictions and complexities of our society gradually build up inside us and find their way into our films, consciously or unconsciously.”

	Speaking of his home country, Alizadeh says the situation in Iran has become “increasingly complex.” “Alongside the difficult economic conditions that have created countless problems for people, to the point where simply getting through everyday life has become almost impossible for the majority, two wars in less than a year, people’s resistance against these attacks, and public protests between the two wars have made the situation in the country even more complicated.”

	“As a result,” he says. “It has become harder for artists to understand and respond to the social conditions around them.” 

	This week, major industry names such as Mark Ruffalo and Tilda Swinton signed a statement shared with Variety that says they are “deeply concerned” by reports of the new prison sentence of five years and one month issued by the Tehran Revolutionary Court against Panahi, as well as the confiscation of his assets, the freezing of his bank accounts, a two-year travel ban and a two-year social media ban.
	

	“Iranian cinema is going through a very difficult period as it tries to redefine its relationship with these circumstances and overcome both internal obstacles, such as the relationship between filmmakers and society, and external ones, particularly censorship,” he goes on. “This makes it harder and slower for new talents to emerge. I believe the most important thing that can help move Iranian cinema forward and create opportunities for new filmmakers is their courage to tell stories while staying true to their own personal voice and style.”

schema.headline: An Iranian Woman Falls Pregnant to Avoid Execution in ‘Inherited’: Situation in Iran Is ‘Increasingly Complex’

title: Kylian Mbappé Impersonator Leads Colorful Roster of Doubles in Egyptian Doc ‘The Lookalike’
description: The growing commotion on the streets near a soccer stadium would easily lead one to believe superstar player Kylian Mbappé himself was signing fan
body:
The growing commotion on the streets near a soccer stadium would easily lead one to believe superstar player Kylian Mbappé himself was signing fan autographs. But, as seen in “The Lookalike,” the furore was not over the French player, but a charismatic impersonator.

	Premiering at the Cairo Film Festival, Nehal Elkoussi’s documentary follows three Egyptians who live in the shadows of their famous lookalikes: Mbappé; Egyptian singer and actor Mohamed Mounir; and late TV preacher Sheikh Mohammed Metwalli Sha’rawi. The doc trails the impersonators as they travel to meet fans, struggle to reconcile their personal and mirrored identities, and reflect on the impact a biological happenstance has had on their lives. The film is produced by Al Jazeera Documentary Channel.
	

	When asked about the inspiration for the project, Elkoussi tells Variety she grew up seeing Mounir impersonators, but was struck by stumbling upon one of her film’s subjects on social media and realizing he did dozens of concerts a month and had built a career around his resemblance to the star. “That was when the idea really clicked into focus: how do these lookalikes become a stand-in for the real star? What drives that? How do they draw in a big audience that sees in them a star within reach? What drives the audience that creates this kind of stardom for them?”

	The director first began developing the project in August of 2024, going on to film for eight months between 2025 and 2026. The experience of following the lookalikes and trying to understand people’s fascination with them came with several “surprises” for the filmmaker.
	

	“I was surprised by the smiles on kids’ faces in the streets whenever they ran into the Mbappé lookalike, reacting as if they were standing right in front of the real Mbappé,” she recalls. “I was surprised by how seriously the Mbappé lookalike took his work, and how committed [he is] as a content creator.”

	The Mbappé impersonator opened a fascinating avenue to “The Lookalike,” as the subject brought with him a whole roster of other soccer star impersonators, from Lionel Messi to Brazil’s goalkeeper Alisson Becker. This also allowed Elkoussi to build on Egypt’s passion for the sport, and its growth in popularity in the Arab region following the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar.



	

					‘The Lookalike’
									Nehal Elkoussi
	



	Elkoussi also realized how class played a big role in people’s attachment to the lookalikes. “The poor needed a lookalike to stand in for the real star they can no longer reach,” she observes. “The people who go to a Mounir lookalike’s concert in a village in Gharbia, or the kids taking photos with the Mbappé lookalike in the street, or those seeking blessings from the El-Shaarawy lookalike, they don’t want a video on a screen. They need to feel that the star or figure is right there with them in flesh and blood, someone they can be near and talk to.”

	According to the director, this human warmth and connection is something “AI can never replace.” “On top of that is their seriousness and dedication to what they do. It’s a daily human effort, hard work, and an attempt to make people happy. It’s unlike technology, which just copies the surface and drains the soul out of it.”

	Premiering at home at the Cairo Film Festival has been a special experience for the filmmaker, particularly because her three subjects made it to the screening. “I made sure to share those moments with them as they’re the real makers of the film,” she says. “They really loved it, and they felt that we captured their lives and who they truly are without passing judgment or criticizing them. Having all of those emotions come back toward the film made me really happy.”

title: How This Year’s Movies From ‘Artificial’ to ‘I Play Rocky’ Turn Political Anxiety Into Compelling Stories
description: For years, Simon Rich wanted to sound the alarm about AI.Rich’s childhood friend Dan Selsam worked as a researcher at OpenAI; Selsam showed Rich, a
body: For years, Simon Rich wanted to sound the alarm about AI.Rich’s childhood friend Dan Selsam worked as a researcher at OpenAI; Selsam showed Rich, a writer known for humorous essays and for the film “An American Pickle,” an early version of the software, and the two friends discussed its ramifications.“It seemed to have real contempt for mankind,” Rich says. “It scared the hell out of me.” Rich published a book, “which was completely ignored,” and found himself striking out in his attempts to get attention with magazine articles. “So, in desperation,” he recalls, “I was like, ‘Maybe if I got a movie star…’”He got Andrew Garfield. In “Artificial,” Garfield plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman as a blithely destructive sociopath who manipulates his way into the center of a potentially civilization-ending technological advance. Rich uses the juicy character to tell a story about the most consequential political issue of the present moment.“I’ve been living with knowledge of this danger for at least five years, due to my fluke friendship with this scientist,” he says. (Selsam issued a public warning about AI’s increasingly uncontrollable behavior in September.) “I wrote this film out of a desperation to communicate to the world this information.”That desperation may be unique to Rich. But the desire to use the tools of screenwriting to illuminate political concerns is certainly not. Had “Artificial” simply been an enumeration of AI’s dangers, it’d likely have attracted as much attention as Rich’s book; instead, it’s a well-told story with a sharp argument at its core. That makes it one of several movies this year that use character and incident — the stuff of quality storytelling — to illuminate their writers’ very real political concerns.That goes for the year’s most-discussed blockbusters: Writer-director Christopher Nolan has imbued “The Odyssey” with a rueful sense of what it means to lose one’s humanity in wartime, while, if it’s anything like its two predecessor films, “Dune: Part Three,” written by Denis Villeneuve and Brian K. Vaughan, promises to examine the uses, and misuses, of power.But it’s showing up across more human-scale dramas this fall, as well. Take “I Play Rocky.” The film depicts the writing and production of “Rocky,” which — before it was an Oscar-winning smash — was the Hail Mary attempt of unknown actor Sylvester Stallone (played by Anthony Ippolito) to write himself a place in the industry. For screenwriter Peter Gamble, the story has resonances well beyond Hollywood history.“‘Rocky’ came out right after the Vietnam War, and it was a time when people needed to believe,” Gamble says. Stallone, in the film’s telling, is the ultimate underdog; Gamble, who himself yearned for a screenwriting breakout, could relate. The message of the film, the writer says, is intended in part for his children: “They’re like, ‘We’re all going to die from global warming. If not, AI is going to kill us next week.’ What power do I have in the universe at all? We need to believe in ourselves again.”American history provides many stories that feel akin to the charged atmosphere of recent years: One, as Gamble notes, is the demoralization of the Vietnam War, and another is the cataclysm of the Great Depression. “The Weight,” written by Matthew Booi and Shelby Gaines, is a rip-roaring adventure film in which unjustly imprisoned convict Samuel Murphy (Ethan Hawke) has the chance to win his freedom by transporting gold bricks across an unruly wilderness. The viewer roots for Murphy in part because he’s compellingly played by a movie star, and in part because the boot under which he struggles looks, at a moment of increased attention to mass incarceration and wealth inequality, familiar.“You don’t want it to be didactic and message-y or preachy in any way,” Gaines says. “But the idea was to try and tell a good story on a personal, individual level and hope that it would echo sympathetically with things that happen on a larger social level — both during the Great Depression and today.” Murphy’s journey depicts the stakes of its historical moment in frankly personal terms — his loss of freedom means the loss of access to his daughter, a crisis the film treats with gravity and righteous anger.“Abstraction doesn’t help you as a writer much,” Gaines says. “If you want to convey something, the heart is the place to start.”Or you can go for the gut. “Ink,” which James Graham adapted from his own stage play, makes the case that Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) and newspaper editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) created the venal media world we live in today. The dawning realization that Lamb, especially, is a force for evil hits particularly hard because Graham has, in the film’s early going, taken pains to make him so charming and his exploits so rootable.“You need these people to surprise you,” Graham says, “so that you want to be in that newsroom — and suddenly, weirdly, for a brief moment, you might even want them to get one over on the establishment.” How did tabloid culture gain such purchase? Because, as the film’s characters make clear, we’re willing to pay for it.“Being Heumann” makes us root for its band of rebels, too — but, in this case, they’re working to bring about a better world. The biopic, written by Sian Heder and Rebekah Taussig, tells the story of Judith Heumann (Ruth Madeley), the activist who led the 1977 demonstration over the government’s failure to enforce disability-rights legislation. By its nature, the film is explicitly political, but its screenplay is also the product of a thoughtful, careful approach to representation and inclusivity.Taussig, who, like the late Heumann, uses a wheelchair, saw a certain power in learning about — and then writing about — the many activists Heumann helped organize. “What was so exciting about the research,” she says, “was this gold mine of learning about these absolutely compelling people.”The first-time screenwriter had grown up seeing “very little disability representation — and [when there was], it always felt so flat. There is a richness to the experience of disability that gets missed if you don’t live it and you can’t portray it.”Taussig’s ability to mine her own insights enriches the film, one that Heder, an Oscar-winner for “CODA,” intended to inspire and delight audiences, as well as educate them. “It’s very important to me that this story reach the widest audience possible,” Heder says, “because the events of the story actually were about a triumph. In a time where a lot of us are feeling really helpless, it was so important to express disabled joy and humor. I wanted to take the audience on a really entertaining ride, where they could leave seeing the world differently.”“Fjord” has a similar reframing effect — though its true-life basis is substantially more downbeat than Judith Heumann’s story. Cristian Mungiu took inspiration from the story of the Bodnariu family, an immigrant couple whose five children were taken away by the Norwegian state amid accusations of child abuse. “Fjord” presents the story of Mihai and Lisbet Gheorghiu (Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve) in a who-do-you-believe social drama, one with painful repercussions.“What I’m looking into, in the stories that I pick up,” Mungiu says, “is this possibility of speaking about something bigger than just that story.” For its writer-director, “Fjord” addresses the painful consequences of globalization, as people from different traditions find that they cannot in fact understand one another. “It’s not a reenactment” of the Bodnariu story, he says: “That’s the starting point of a story in which everything is structured to speak about the relationship between the majority and the individual.”“Fjord” won the top prize at this year’s Cannes; the runner-up, “Minotaur,” also places a family drama in counterpoint with a story of major import. Here, a story of marital infidelity (based on Claude Chabrol’s 1969 film “The Unfaithful Wife”) plays out in 2022 as Russia is scaling up its military actions against Ukraine.Writer-director Andrey Zvyagintsev had been working to put the film together for years — and, as he wrote, the mobilization against Ukraine was all over the news. “It was a very logical thing,” he says through a translator. “I started to fill gaps in the script with the realities of what was happening.” Like Simon Rich trying to spread the word against AI, Zvyagintsev used his script to convey what he was hearing, like local mayors asking businesspeople to choose which of their employees will be conscripted. “This is not something I took from the air,” Zvyagintsev says. “This is real information that came by phone. People would be afraid to speak up about those situations.”For Zvyagintsev, this use of character to explore the world around him is what screenwriting is all about. “The whole ocean,” he says, “can be reflected in one ocean drop.”

schema.headline: How This Year’s Movies From ‘Artificial’ to ‘I Play Rocky’ Turn Political Anxiety Into Compelling Stories

title: OsamaSon Concert: Multiple People Injured In Crowd Crush Caught on Video
body:

              OsamaSon's sold-out rap concert at NYC's Terminal 5 turned into utter chaos Thursday night, following a crowd crush that left 4 people injured -- and it was all caught on video.

title: Trump Defends Stephen Miller After Future House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries Calls Him 'Racist'
description:
President Trump
                          Defends Stephen Miller After Hakeem Jeffries Calls Him
body:
President Trump
                          Defends Stephen Miller After Hakeem Jeffries Calls Him 'Racist'
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 21, 2026
                            10:03 AM PST
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
              President Donald Trump is pushing back on Hakeem Jeffries' claims that his White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller is racist ... arguing he had to be "strong on the border."
      
    
              Speaking with Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany on "Saturday in America," Trump said ... "So he called him a racist. But we had to be strong. They allowed 25 million people and killers, murderers. They allowed drug dealers and rapists into our country."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              The incoming speaker of the House previously told the New York Times ... "I made it clear that Stephen Miller's a stone-cold racist. Why would I deal with him at this point in time?"
      

              Jeffries added that Miller was "the architect of Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine," saying there was cruelty, chaos, and death tied to his policies.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Trump, for his part, was surprisingly complimentary of Jeffries during his chat, saying he called the Democrat to congratulate him after the blue wave in the most recent midterm elections secured his spot as speaker in January.
      
    
              The prez claimed that he and Jeffries could still work together, adding ... "What he did is pretty spectacular with getting that position. And it’s nice -- first Black person in that position. It's a big deal."
